lead: Water looks identical in a glass whatever is dissolved in it. This unit gives you the numbers that describe what is in water, the standards it must meet, and the engineering that turns raw water into boiler feed or drinking water. After it you can compute hardness as CaCO₃, size a lime-soda dose, follow a city treatment train, and choose between reverse osmosis and electrodialysis for a given salt load.
about: The unit starts at the measuring bench. 7.1 defines the parameters — turbidity, pH, TDS, BOD, coliforms — and condenses calcium and magnesium into one number, hardness as CaCO₃. 7.2 carries that hardness into an industrial boiler, where it turns into scale, sludge, corrosion and embrittlement, and shows the softening routes that remove it first. 7.3 moves to city scale: coagulation, settling, filtration and disinfection, the sequence a plant runs every day. 7.4 handles water too salty for either route, comparing reverse osmosis, driven by pressure, with electrodialysis, driven by voltage. Each chapter reuses the number produced by the one before.

chapters.idea: Water quality is a short list of measured numbers, and hardness is the single number that expresses Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ as CaCO₃.
chapters.depth: Physical parameters with units: turbidity (NTU), colour, odour, temperature. Chemical: pH, TDS (mg/L), conductivity (µS/cm), chloride, sulphate, nitrate, fluoride, iron, dissolved oxygen, BOD and COD (mg/L). Biological: coliform count by MPN. Drinking water limits from BIS 10500, given as acceptable and permissible pairs — pH 6.5–8.5, total hardness 200/600, TDS 500/2000, fluoride 1.0/1.5 mg/L. Then hardness: temporary (carbonate) and permanent (non-carbonate), units of mg/L as CaCO₃, ppm, meq/L, °Clark and °French, with conversions (1 meq/L = 50 mg/L as CaCO₃). Core formula: hardness as CaCO₃ = (mass of ion in mg/L) × 50 ÷ equivalent weight of the ion. Classification: soft below 60, moderately hard 60–120, hard 120–180, very hard above 180 mg/L as CaCO₃. Determination by EDTA titration at pH 10 with Eriochrome Black T. Only a few universities examine this chapter in full; the depth that matters is the calculation, not instrument detail.

figure.title: From sample to verdict
figure.aria: A sample splits into physical, chemical and biological tests; the tests feed a comparison against BIS 10500 limits, and the chemical branch separately produces a hardness value in CaCO₃ units.

chapters.example: A groundwater sample contains Ca²⁺ = 80 mg/L and Mg²⁺ = 24 mg/L, with no other hardness-causing ions. Find the total hardness as CaCO₃ in mg/L and in meq/L, and say whether it meets the BIS acceptable limit of 200 mg/L. Take equivalent weights Ca²⁺ = 20, Mg²⁺ = 12, CaCO₃ = 50. Solution: Ca²⁺ contributes 80 × 50 ÷ 20 = 200 mg/L; Mg²⁺ contributes 24 × 50 ÷ 12 = 100 mg/L; total = 300 mg/L as CaCO₃ = 300 ÷ 50 = 6 meq/L. It is above the acceptable 200 but below the permissible 600, so the water is used only when no better source exists.
chapters.trap: Quoting the ion's own mg/L as if it were already hardness, and using the molecular weight 100 of CaCO₃ instead of its equivalent weight 50.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (coordination compounds) explains why EDTA holds Ca²⁺ tightly at pH 10; here it is only a method, not re-taught.
chapters.leave: Softening and boiler troubles to 7.2, plant-scale treatment to 7.3, salt removal to 7.4; the full BOD/COD procedure and instrumental analysis to a laboratory course.

chapters.idea: Every boiler trouble comes from a named impurity, and every remedy either removes that impurity before the boiler or controls it inside.
chapters.depth: Feed water requirements: near-zero hardness, low dissolved oxygen, pH held near 10–11, low silica, controlled alkalinity. Troubles, each with cause, effect and cure: scale (CaCO₃, CaSO₄, Mg(OH)₂, silica — poor heat transfer, overheated tubes, wasted fuel); sludge (loose precipitate, removed by blowdown); corrosion (O₂, CO₂ and acid attack, pitting); caustic embrittlement (NaOH concentrating in crevices, cracking near rivets and bends); carryover — priming and foaming from high alkalinity, oil and suspended solids. External softening: lime-soda process (cold and hot, with equations), zeolite or ion-exchange process with NaCl regeneration, demineralisation with cation and anion resins in two-bed and mixed-bed form. Internal conditioning: phosphate, carbonate, calgon (sodium hexametaphosphate) and colloidal conditioning; deaeration, mechanical and chemical (hydrazine, sodium sulphite); blowdown. Include the lime and soda requirement formulas with equivalents of CaO (56), Ca(OH)₂ (74), Na₂CO₃ (106) and CaCO₃ (100). Some syllabi call the chapter internal treatment of water. Only a few universities examine the dosing arithmetic.

figure.aria: A tree headed boiler water problems branching into scale, sludge, corrosion, caustic embrittlement and carryover, each carrying its cause and one matching remedy.

chapters.example: A boiler feed water contains free CO₂ = 44 mg/L, calcium bicarbonate hardness = 100 mg/L as CaCO₃, magnesium bicarbonate hardness = 50 mg/L as CaCO₃, and calcium sulphate hardness = 80 mg/L as CaCO₃. Calculate the lime (as CaO) and soda (as Na₂CO₃) needed for 1000 L. Solution: CO₂ as CaCO₃ = 44 × 50 ÷ 22 = 100 mg/L. Lime = (56 ÷ 100) × (CO₂ + Ca(HCO₃)₂ + 2 × Mg(HCO₃)₂) = 0.56 × (100 + 100 + 100) = 168 mg/L as CaO. Soda = (106 ÷ 100) × non-carbonate hardness remaining after lime = 1.06 × 80 = 84.8 mg/L as Na₂CO₃. For 1000 L: 168 g lime and 84.8 g soda.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the factor 2 on Mg(HCO₃)₂ in the lime formula, and mixing the masses of CaO, Ca(OH)₂, CaCO₃ and Na₂CO₃ without converting through equivalents.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1 — hardness as CaCO₃ and its units are the input to every dose calculation here.
chapters.leave: Corrosion mechanisms and cathodic protection to Unit 4; disinfection and clarification to 7.3; membrane demineralisation to 7.4.

chapters.idea: A city plant is a fixed train of steps, each removing one class of impurity, ending in a disinfection step that leaves a protective residual.
chapters.depth: Intake and coarse and fine screens. Aeration, which oxidises Fe²⁺ and Mn²⁺ to insoluble oxides, strips CO₂ and odour. Coagulation with alum (Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O), ferric chloride or polyaluminium chloride, with the role of alkalinity and added lime, and the pH band where the floc forms best. Slow mixing (flocculation) to grow the floc, then sedimentation; settling velocity from Stokes' law, v = d²(ρ_p − ρ)g ÷ 18η, with each symbol named. Filtration: slow sand beds at 0.1–0.3 m/h with a biological layer, rapid sand beds at 4–8 m/h with backwashing. Disinfection: chlorine chemistry with HOCl and OCl⁻ in equilibrium, the breakpoint curve, chloramines, ozone, UV, and the residual of 0.2–0.5 mg/L carried to the taps. Bleaching powder dosing using its available chlorine percentage. A few universities teach this chapter; keep the emphasis on the sequence and the dose arithmetic, not plant drawings.

figure.title: Municipal treatment train
figure.aria: A vertical chain running from raw water through screening, aeration, coagulation, settling and sand filtration to disinfection and clear water, with the alum dose and the chlorine residual picked out.

chapters.example: A service reservoir holds 50,000 L of filtered water. The required dose is 0.5 mg/L of available chlorine, and the bleaching powder in stock is 30% available chlorine. Find the mass of bleaching powder to add. Solution: chlorine needed = 0.5 mg/L × 50,000 L = 25,000 mg = 25 g. Bleaching powder needed = 25 ÷ 0.30 = 83.3 g.
chapters.trap: Treating the coagulant dose and the chlorine dose as the same quantity, and forgetting to divide by the available-chlorine fraction so that the powder mass comes out too small.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1 — turbidity, coliform and pH limits are the targets the train must meet; Stokes' law needs the viscosity idea from fluid mechanics.
chapters.leave: Hardness removal to 7.2; dissolved-salt removal to 7.4; disinfection kinetics and breakpoint curve modelling to a later course.

chapters.idea: Reverse osmosis pushes water through a membrane with pressure above the osmotic pressure; electrodialysis pulls the ions themselves through membranes with a DC field.
chapters.depth: Why desalination is needed: TDS and chloride limits from 7.1 that ordinary treatment cannot reach. Reverse osmosis: semipermeable membrane, osmotic pressure from van 't Hoff's law π = iCRT with every symbol named, applied pressure above π, recovery and the rise of brine concentration along the module, flux, spiral-wound modules, cellulose acetate and polyamide thin-film composite membranes, pretreatment for scaling and fouling. Working pressures of roughly 15–30 bar for brackish water and 50–80 bar for seawater. Electrodialysis: alternating cation-exchange and anion-exchange membranes, a DC field, ion-depleted and ion-concentrated compartments, the stack, polarity reversal to control fouling, best for brackish water and uneconomical at seawater strength because energy scales with salt removed. One line each on thermal desalination by multi-stage flash. A comparison table of the two processes on feed TDS, driving force, energy and fouling. Only a few universities teach this chapter; keep to the principle and the osmotic pressure sum.

figure.title: Reverse osmosis
figure.aria: A down-flow diagram in which pretreated sea water is pumped to about 60 bar into the membrane module, which splits into a low-salt permeate and a brine reject.

chapters.example: Sea water is modelled as 0.5 mol/L NaCl at 300 K, with i = 2 and R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). Find the osmotic pressure and the minimum feed pressure for reverse osmosis. Solution: π = iCRT = 2 × 0.5 × 0.0821 × 300 = 24.6 atm, about 25 bar. Water crosses the membrane only when the applied pressure exceeds π, so the feed must be pushed above roughly 25 bar; real seawater plants run at 50–80 bar because recovery concentrates the brine and the pressure drop along the module adds to the requirement.
chapters.trap: Using π itself as the operating pressure instead of a pressure above it, and ignoring that recovery raises brine concentration so the osmotic pressure rises along the module.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1 for the TDS limit; Unit 4 (electrochemistry) for ions, conductivity and transport under a field, which is what electrodialysis uses.
chapters.leave: Thermal desalination beyond one line; membrane polymer structure to Unit 5; pump and energy economics to a mechanical or civil course.
